newsitem.title: USA: Thousands flee homes as floods hit western U.S.
newsitem.headline: Thousands flee homes as floods hit western U.S.

text.p: Thousands fled their homes, gambling casinos were sandbagged and 2,300 people were stranded in Yosemite National Park as floods and mudslides hit the rain-soaked western United States on Thursday.

California Gov. Pete Wilson declared a state of emergency in 25 counties, covering most of the state north of San Francisco, as rivers swelled by days of heavy rain flooded or threatened to burst their banks. The declaration makes the counties eligible for state aid.
Powerful storms, which have caused havoc in Washington state and Oregon for the last week, hammered California, Nevada and Idaho, leaving a trail of floods, mudslides, power outages and closed roads.

In Nevada, the normally placid Truckee river overflowed, causing the worst flooding in downtown Reno in more than 40 years. A fast-moving torrent of murky brown water swept through homes and businesses, leaving a basketball net just poking out above the flood.

Several Reno hotel-casinos were forced to close and evacuate guests, but in others, the gambling went on in sandbagged casinos. Runways at the Reno-Tahoe airport were submerged and several airliners stood in water.
After touring the area by helicopter, Nevada Gov. Bob Miller, who declared a state of emergency in four counties, said damage could be in the hundreds of millions of dollars.

"It's clear to say this is the most significant flood damage in the history of Nevada in terms of financial cost," he said. Miller said he had contacted the Federal Emergency Management Agency in hopes of getting speedy approval for federal aid for flood victims.

American Red Cross spokeswoman Wendy Perrotti said 18,100 evacuees were housed in 55 Red Cross shelters in California, Idaho, Nevada, Oregon and Washington. The vast majority -- 17,600 people -- were at shelters in California's central valley and the Sacramento area, she said.
Some 6,000 residents of Yuba City, 40 miles (70 kms) northeast of Sacramento, came to a local shelter under a voluntary evacuation after the Feather River reached flood stage, she said.
"It's an enormous disaster. We are pulling in resources from all over," she said.

Several hundred evacuees spent Wednesday night at shelters in northern California's wine country, where the Russian and Napa rivers broke their banks, flooding the town of Guerneville and inundating vineyards.
Emergency officials advised the 4,000 residents of the Pajaro area in central California to evacuate as soon as possible because the Pajaro River was nearing flood stage.

Oregon Gov. John Kitzhaber declared emergencies in five storm-hit counties and mobilized 200 National Guard troops to help with transportation, traffic control and sandbagging. Gov. Mike Lowry has declared a state of emergency in 19 Washington counties.
At least 14 deaths are blamed on the storms, estimated to have caused up to $250 million in property damage in Washington, Oregon and northern California.

Three hikers missing in the Mount Shasta area of northern California were found alive and well on Thursday, the Siskiyou County Sheriff's Department said. A search went on for another three hikers missing in Snohomish County northeast of Seattle.
About 2,300 tourists, park workers and their families were stranded in California's scenic Yosemite National Park, 150 miles (240 km) southeast of San Francisco, officials said.
Heavy rain pushed the Merced River over its banks, closing all highways into Yosemite Valley, where the park headquarters and accommodation are located, they said.

Park spokesman Kendell Thompson said there were about 1,100 tourists in Yosemite Valley and about 1,200 staff and their families. Rooms were available for all the guests and park employees had homes in the valley, he said.
"They are warm and dry. There is enough food. The electricity is still on. Everybody is in good shape," he said. He said it was a "top priority" to find a way to evacuate people from the park.

Alister Bull, a Reuters correspondent vacationing in the park, said he had been planning to leave Yosemite on Thursday but was prevented from doing so because the roads were under water and closed. "We are literally marooned. There is three feet of water across the road on both sides of us," he said.

Bull said guests were handed a park bulletin stating that the National Parks Service was planning an emergency air evacuation of all guests from Yosemite Valley. It said evacuation may be necessary "due to a complete failure of Yosemite Valley sewer system." However, a park spokeswoman said bad weather had ruled out an air evacuation for now.

About 19,000 homes and business in northern and central California were without electricity because of the storm and about 13,600 customers remained cut off in the Seattle area, utility officials said.
